```{r binned_population}
m0 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)), data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
m1 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ POPULATION_binned + offset(log(EXP)), data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
chisq_result <- anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Is the effect of POPULATION_binned significant at 95%% confidence? %s", ifelse(chisq_result$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No")))
plot_freq_sev(data_enriched, "POPULATION_binned")
```

The variable is significant at 95% confidence. We see that the 2 largest population bins have very similar claim frequencies, however, merging them would remove the distinction between these two bins that we see for the average claim cost.

#### Regions

We will check the significance and claim frequency across regions

```{r municipality_region_significance}
m0 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)), data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
m1 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)) + REGION, data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
    test_result <- anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq")
    cat(sprintf("Is variable %s significant? %s\n", "REGION", ifelse(test_result$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < test_level, "Yes", "No")))
plot_freq_sev(data_enriched, "REGION")
```

It is clear that the Brussels region has a distinct claim frequency and severity pattern compared to the other regions. It is interesting to note that the frequency is higher while the severity is lower, which aligns with our hypothesis about urban areas.
We'll test if it makes sense to keep the Walloon and Flemish regions separated as well or not (as before, the test is made on the claim frequency using a chi-squared test).

```{r region_significance}
merged_regions <- fct_collapse(
    data_enriched$REGION,
    "Brussels" = c("RÉGION DE BRUXELLES-CAPITALE"),
    "Others" = c("RÉGION WALLONNE", "RÉGION FLAMANDE"),
)
data_enriched$REGION_merged <- merged_regions
m0 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)) + REGION, data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
m1 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)) + REGION_merged, data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
test_result <- anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Was it justified to merge the REGION bins? %s", ifelse(test_result$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < test_level, "No", "Yes")))
plot_freq_sev(data_enriched, "REGION_merged")
```

We see that despite a much lower exposure in Brussels, the claim frequency is significantly higher from the other regions. The severity, although not significantly because of high variability, appears to be lower in Brussels compared to the other regions.
This confirms our hypothesis that urban areas, such as Brussels, tend to have a higher claim frequency compared to less densely populated regions but that these accidents tend to have a lower severity:

```{r severity_by_region}
urb_rur_comp <- data_enriched %>%
    group_by(REGION_merged) %>%
    summarise(
        total_exposure = sum(EXP),
        total_claims = sum(NCLAIMS),
        total_claim_amount = sum(AMOUNT),
        frequency = total_claims / total_exposure,
        severity = total_claim_amount / total_claims,
        expected_claims = frequency * severity
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(frequency)) 
urb_rur_comp %>%
    kable(
        caption = "Expected claims by merged region\nSplit by frequency and severity",
        align = "l", booktabs = TRUE
    )
```

With this quick descriptive analysis, we can confirm that in our sample:

- The claim frequency is higher in urban areas like Brussels compared to other regions (factor `r urb_rur_comp$frequency[urb_rur_comp$REGION_merged == "Brussels"]/urb_rur_comp$frequency[urb_rur_comp$REGION_merged == "Others"]`)
- The claim severity is lower in urban areas like Brussels compared to other regions (factor `r urb_rur_comp$severity[urb_rur_comp$REGION_merged == "Brussels"]/urb_rur_comp$severity[urb_rur_comp$REGION_merged == "Others"]`)
- The frequency effect outweighs the severity effect in determining the expected claims between urban and other regions (factor `r urb_rur_comp$expected_claims[urb_rur_comp$REGION_merged == "Brussels"]/urb_rur_comp$expected_claims[urb_rur_comp$REGION_merged == "Others"]`)

We expect to see similar effects for other granularities, such as municipalities, where urban areas may exhibit higher claim frequencies but lower severities compared to less densely populated areas.

#### Municipalities

There are far too many municipalities to use it as a simple categorical variable in our models. Hierachical credibility are out of scope. We can thus focus on the n largest municipalities by exposure and group the remaining ones into an "Other" category.

```{r municipalities_aggregation}
data_enriched %>%
    group_by(MUNICIPALITY) %>%
    summarise(
        total_exposure = sum(EXP)
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(total_exposure)) %>% head(n=30) %>%
    mutate(category = ifelse(row_number() <= 6, "Selected", "Other")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = reorder(MUNICIPALITY, -total_exposure), y = total_exposure, fill = category)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Selected" = "steelblue", "Other" = "lightgrey")) +
    labs(x = "Municipality", y = "Total Exposure", fill = "Category", title = "Top 30 Municipalities by Exposure") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

We can focus on the 6 largest municipalities by exposure before the exposure distribution flattens out.

```{r top_municipalities}
exp_breakpoint <- data_enriched %>%
    group_by(MUNICIPALITY) %>%
    summarise(
        total_exposure = sum(EXP)
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(total_exposure)) %>%
    head(n=6) 
data_enriched$MUNICIPALITY_binned <- ifelse(data_enriched$MUNICIPALITY %in% exp_breakpoint$MUNICIPALITY, as.character(data_enriched$MUNICIPALITY), "Other")
data_enriched$MUNICIPALITY_binned <- factor(data_enriched$MUNICIPALITY_binned) %>% fct_infreq()

plot_freq_sev(data_enriched, "MUNICIPALITY_binned")
m0 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)), data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
m1 <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ MUNICIPALITY_binned + offset(log(EXP)), data = data_enriched, family = poisson(link = "log"))
results <- anova(m0, m1, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Is variable %s significant? %s\n", "MUNICIPALITY_binned", ifelse(results$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < test_level, "Yes", "No")))
```

We now have a binned version of the MUNICIPALITY variable which is significant and usable in our model. Of course, the exposure is limited even in the bigger municipalities and that causes some variability in the frequency estimates.
However, for the sake of interpretation, we'll keep the cities separated even though Charleroi and Antwerp are similar in terms of frequency and so are Gand and Liège.
We seem to capture a similar phenomenon with cities having a higher claim frequency compared to smaller municipalities even if the effect is less clear than for the regions.
What is also striking is that average claim cost is much higher in Charleroi than anywhere else.

```{r desc_top_municipalities}
data_enriched %>%
    group_by(MUNICIPALITY_binned) %>%
    summarise(
        total_claims = sum(NCLAIMS),
        total_exposure = sum(EXP),
        total_claim_amount = sum(AMOUNT),
        frequency = total_claims / total_exposure,
        severity = total_claim_amount / total_claims,
        expected_claims = frequency * severity
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(frequency)) %>%
    kable(
        caption = "Expected claims by municipality\nSplit by frequency and severity",,
        align = "l", booktabs = TRUE
    )
```

Even if some cities follow the high frequency, low severity pattern, we do find outliers such as Charleroi where the severity is unusually high or Liège where it falls unusually low.
We then seem to capture something more than the simple urban-rural divide which justifies keeping the `MUNICIPALITY_binned` variable in our model.

[^projection]: Coordinate Reference System are identifiers to explain how the projection from a 3D sphere to a 2D plane is performed. The Belgian Lambert 2008 (3812) projection is commonly used for visualizing geographical data in Belgium.

### Polynomial Features

For the five numerical variables, we will consider the polynomial features up to the third degree to capture potential non-linear relationships with the response variable.
This is an intermediate step towards the GAM models where we will explicitly model non-linear effects.
Note that:
- We will use Pearson correlation (continuous variables) instead of Spearman correlation because the rank-rank approach won't help us differentiate between the polynomial features of the same positive variable (ranks are maintained).
- We will look at the p-values of the correlation tests instead of the correlation coefficients themselves to assess the significance of the relationships.
- For the correlation with average claim amount (`AVG`), we will only consider the claims where `NCLAIMS` is greater than zero.
- Orthogonal polynomial features will be considered separately to avoid multicollinearity issues inherent in raw polynomial features.
- To compute orthogonal polynomial features, we will filter out the NA values from the data.

```{r polynomial_features}
numerical_continuous <- c("BM", "AGEPH", "AGEC", "POWER", "POPULATION")

polynomial_features <- lapply(numerical_continuous, function(var) {
    poly(data_enriched[[var]], degree = 3, raw = TRUE)
})
names(polynomial_features) <- numerical_continuous
correlation_matrix <- data.frame(
    matrix(NA, nrow = length(numerical_continuous), ncol = 6)
)
rownames(correlation_matrix) <- numerical_continuous
colnames(correlation_matrix) <- c(
    "Claims Poly1", "Claims Poly2", "Claims Poly3",
    "Avg Poly1", "Avg Poly2", "Avg Poly3")

for (var in numerical_continuous) {
    poly_values <- polynomial_features[[var]]
    for (j in 1:3) {
        correlation_matrix[var, j] <- cor.test(data_enriched[["NCLAIMS"]], poly_values[, j], method = "pearson")$p.value
        claims_only_avg <- data_enriched[["AVG"]][data_enriched[["NCLAIMS"]] > 0]
        claims_only_poly_values <- poly_values[data_enriched[["NCLAIMS"]] > 0, j]
        correlation_matrix[var, j + 3] <- cor.test(claims_only_avg, claims_only_poly_values, method = "pearson")$p.value
    }
}

pheatmap(correlation_matrix,
    main = "Correlation P-Values Heatmap - Polynomial Features\n(Green = Significant p<0.05, Red = Non-significant)",
    display_numbers = TRUE,
    number_format = "%.4f",
    breaks = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 1),
    color = c("lightgreen", "white", "lightcoral"),
    legend = FALSE,
    cluster_rows = FALSE,
    cluster_cols = FALSE
)
```

We first notice that `AGEC` is not significantly correlated with `NCLAIMS` when considered with the first and second-degree polynomial features.
As we saw before, the non-linear effect for this variable is captured in our WoE binning. An alternative approach could have been to use the third-degree polynomial.
We would still have the issue of fixed effects being imposed by the polynomial terms, which might not fully capture the underlying non-linear relationship.
This is a good example of why binning can sometimes be more flexible in capturing non-linear relationships compared to fixed polynomial terms.

We notice that the correllations between the polynomial features of a same variable are similar, this is foreseeable given that higher-degree polynomials are derived from the lower-degree ones.
We are here exposed to multicollinearity issues. A solution is to check the **orthogonal polynomial features** instead of the raw ones, as they are uncorrelated by construction.
This also enables us to differentiate the individual contributions of each polynomial term more clearly in the modeling process (linear, quadratic, cubic).

```{r orthogonal_polynomial_features}

no_na <- na.omit(data_enriched)
orthogonal_polynomial_features <- lapply(numerical_continuous, function(var) {
    poly(no_na[[var]], degree = 3, raw = FALSE)
})
names(orthogonal_polynomial_features) <- numerical_continuous
orth_correlation_matrix <- data.frame(
    matrix(NA, nrow = length(numerical_continuous), ncol = 6)
)
rownames(orth_correlation_matrix) <- numerical_continuous
colnames(orth_correlation_matrix) <- c(
    "OrthClaims Poly1", "OrthClaims Poly2", "OrthClaims Poly3",
    "OrthAvg Poly1", "OrthAvg Poly2", "OrthAvg Poly3")

for (var in numerical_continuous) {
    poly_values <- orthogonal_polynomial_features[[var]]
    for (j in 1:3) {
        orth_correlation_matrix[var, j] <- cor.test(no_na[["NCLAIMS"]], poly_values[, j], method = "pearson")$p.value
        claims_only_avg <- no_na[["AVG"]][no_na[["NCLAIMS"]] > 0]
        claims_only_poly_values <- poly_values[no_na[["NCLAIMS"]] > 0, j]
        orth_correlation_matrix[var, j + 3] <- cor.test(claims_only_avg, claims_only_poly_values, method = "pearson")$p.value
    }
}

pheatmap(orth_correlation_matrix,
    main = "Correlation P-Values Heatmap - Orthogonal Polynomial Features\n(Green = Significant p<0.05, Red = Non-significant)",
    display_numbers = TRUE,
    number_format = "%.4f",
    breaks = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 1),
    color = c("lightgreen", "white", "lightcoral"),
    legend = FALSE,
    cluster_rows = FALSE,
    cluster_cols = FALSE
) 
```

From this orthogonal polynomial feature exploration we can conclude that:

- Polynomial features are more significantly correlated with the number of claims (`NCLAIMS`) than with the average claim amount (`AVG`) which can simply be due to lesser observations for the latter.
- Orthogonal polynomial features help assess whether each polynomial term contributes significantly to the relationship with the target variables, without being confounded by multicollinearity. This will serve as benchmark to the smoothing functions in the GAM models.

In conclusion, polynomials are a way to capture non-linear relationships. However, the incremental effect of these polynomial terms is still fixed in a GLM.
We therefore prefer working with binned features rather than relying solely on polynomial terms.
We will nevertheless see if the smoothing functions of the GAM models confirm the conclusions drawn from our exploratory analysis.

### Interaction Features

Interactions are usually added as a result of business knowledge. In our case, we know from a theorical background that the age of the policyholder interacts with the power of the car.
We can add this interaction effect and test its significance in our models. Instead of manually testing all possible combinations. We'll use a decision tree approach which nature is to look for interactions and splits that best explain the variability in the target variable.
With a shallow decision tree (depth of 3), we can identify the most relevant interactions without overfitting the data.
Watch out the decision trees are not robusts and can be sensitive to small changes in the data. We'll do a 10-fold cross-validation to mitigate this issue.

```{r interaction-tree}

tree_model <- rpart(
    NCLAIMS ~ COVERAGE + FUEL + FLEET + SEX + # Categorical features
    BM_binned + AGEPH_binned_merged + AGEC_binned + POWER_binned_merged + # Binned numerical features
    POPULATION_binned + REGION_merged + MUNICIPALITY_binned, # Enriched features
    data = data_enriched,
    method = "poisson",
    control = rpart.control(maxdepth = 3, xval = 10, cp = 0)
)
rpart.plot(tree_model)

importance_df <- data.frame(
    feature = names(tree_model$variable.importance),
    importance = tree_model$variable.importance %>% `/`(sum(.))
)
importance_df <- importance_df %>% arrange(desc(importance))

ggplot(importance_df, aes(x = reorder(feature, importance), y = importance)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = "Feature Importance in Decision Tree",
            x = "Feature",
            y = "Importance Score") +
    theme_minimal()
```

Based on this machine learning approach, we can identify both specific interactions and the most important features that influence the target variable. When adding interaction terms to our models, we can thus consider:

**Specific Interactions:** representing the two first splits identified by the decision tree.

- `BM_binned.[0,1]` x `FUEL.gasoline`
- `BM_binned.[0,1]` x `!FUEL.gasoline`
- `!BM_binned.[0,1]` x `REGION_merged.Others`: will not add it as it is captured below already
- `!BM_binned.[0,1]` x `!REGION_merged.Others`: will not add it as it is captured below already

```{r specific-interactions}
data_enriched <- data_enriched %>%
    mutate(
        BM_01_FUEL_gasoline = BM_binned == "[0,1]" & FUEL == "gasoline",
        BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline = BM_binned == "[0,1]" & FUEL != "gasoline"
    )
```

**Variable Interactions:** representing the 3 most important features identified by the decision tree.

- `BM_binned` x `AGEPH_binned_merged`
- `REGION_merged` x `POWER_binned_merged`
- `BM_binned` x `REGION_merged`

This concludes the feature engineering and more generally the data preparation phase. We now have a set of enriched, transformed, binned, and merged features ready for the modelling phase.
We will start the next section by listing this set of variables and looking at the reference class.

# Frequency Modeling

Now that we have explored, transformed, and enriched our data. We are ready to proceed with the modelling phase. As described in the Approach section of the Introduction, we will go from the null model (with the offset only) towards more complex models by gradually incorporating features and keeping the significant ones.
Below is a list of the variables and their 5 first levels per layer of complexity.

```{r prep_modelling}
# Clean intermediary objects not used for modelling
functions <- ls()[sapply(ls(), function(x) is.function(get(x)))]
rm(list = setdiff(ls(), c(
    "data", "data_enriched", "holdout", "mtpl_be",
    "conv_matching", "refnis", "pop", 
    "result_named_list", "n_bins_named_list",
    functions)))
cat(sprintf("Remaining objects and functions: %s", paste(ls(), collapse = ", ")))

# Save remaining objects for modelling
save(list = ls(), file = "../data/modelling_objects.RData")
```


```{r start_modelling}
load("../data/modelling_objects.RData")

original_categorical_features <- c("COVERAGE", "FUEL", "FLEET", "SEX")
continuous_features <- c("BM", "AGEPH", "AGEC", "POWER")
binned_continuous_features <- c("BM_binned", "AGEPH_binned_merged", "AGEC_binned", "POWER_binned_merged")
enriched_features <- c("REGION_merged", "MUNICIPALITY_binned", "POPULATION")
binned_enriched_features <- c("REGION_merged", "MUNICIPALITY_binned", "POPULATION_binned")
interaction_features <- c("BM_01_FUEL_gasoline", "BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline", "BM_binned:AGEPH_binned_merged", "REGION_merged:AGEPH_binned_merged", "BM_binned:REGION_merged")

levels_named_list <- list()
for (col in c(original_categorical_features, binned_continuous_features, binned_enriched_features)) {
    if (!col %in% colnames(data_enriched)) {stop(sprintf("Column %s is missing from data_enriched", col))}
    levels_named_list[[col]] <- levels(data_enriched[[col]])
}
```

**Original Categorical Features:**
Note that `USE` was excluded because it was not statistically significant in preliminary analyses. The variables for the first set of predictors are:

```{r original_categorical_features}
for (col in original_categorical_features) {
    cat(sprintf("Levels for %s: %s\n", col, paste(head(levels_named_list[[col]],5), collapse = ", ")))
}
```

The reference levels will thus represent male policyholders with a third-party liability coverage only for a gasoline-fueled vehicle which is not part of a fleet.

**Continuous Features:**
The continuous features as such will be included in the GAM models only. We binned and merged them into categorical variables for the GLM modelling.

```{r binned_continuous_features}
for (col in binned_continuous_features) {
    cat(sprintf("Levels for %s: %s\n", col, paste(head(levels_named_list[[col]],5), collapse = ", ")))
}
```

The reference levels are here defined by the first level of each binned continuous feature. We therefore have a policyholder between 18 and 24 years old with a new car (less than 1 year old) of 10 to 33 kilowatts of power and a bonus-malus score of 0.

**Enriched Features:**
Based on geospation information, we have created, binned and merged both categorical and continuous features to capture urban/rural distinctions and municipality-level characteristics.

```{r binned_enriched_features}
for (col in binned_enriched_features) {
    cat(sprintf("Levels for %s: %s\n", col, paste(head(levels_named_list[[col]],5), collapse = ", ")))
}
```

The reference for these enriched features is a policyholder living in a small municipality (995 to 7680 inhabitants) outside of Brussels and the other main urban areas.

**Interaction Features:**
We have also created specific and variable interaction features based on expert knowledge and the decision tree analysis.

- `POWER_binned_merged` x `AGEPH_binned_merged`: expert knowledge
- `BM_01_FUEL_gasoline`: specific interaction based on decision tree analysis
- `BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline`: specific interaction based on decision tree analysis
- `BM_binned` x `AGEPH_binned_merged`: variable interaction based on feature importance
- `REGION_merged` x `AGEPH_binned_merged`: variable interaction based on feature importance
- `BM_binned` x `REGION_merged`: variable interaction based on feature importance

**Polynomial Features:**
We also considered raw and orthogonal polynomial features for the continuous variables to capture potential non-linear relationships in the GAM models.
We decided not to include them in the GLM models for the sake of model simplicity and interpretability. These polynomial effects will be naturally captured in the GAM models through the smooth functions.
We will then be able to see whether the GAM results confirm our exploratory analysis.

## Validation Framework

The modelling exercise will be conducted on our training dataset, while keeping the holdout set separate for final model validation. 
In this section, we will create a workflow that encompasses both data preparation and model selection steps (including cross-validation).

- **Data Preparation**: starting from the enriched dataset, applying necessary transformations as described in the data preparation section.
- **Performance Evaluation**: the correct performance metrics need to be optimized for in order to pick the best model and avoid overfitting.
- **Model Workflow**: the complete modeling workflow will then be specified separately for frequence and severity and for GLM and GAM models in the next sections.

### Data Preparation Workflow

The preparation recipe uses `step_mutate()` to bin continuous variables, merge factor levels, and create the specific interaction indicators. 
The saved `levels_named_list` defines the complete factor order. Then `step_relevel()` explicitly sets each reference level.
Bin boundaries and levels remain fixed at their previously selected values when baking new data, which need not contain observations in every bin. 
Geographic enrichment remains a separate join before the recipe.

```{r data_prep_workflow}
# Data enrichment

data_enrichment <- function(input_data) {
    if (!("PC" %in% colnames(input_data))) {stop("PC column is missing from raw_data")}
    if (!("ID" %in% colnames(input_data))) {stop("ID column is missing from raw_data")}
    if (!exists("conv_matching")) {stop("conv_matching object is missing")}
    if (!exists("refnis")) {stop("refnis object is missing")}
    if (!exists("pop")) {stop("pop object is missing")}
    output_data <- input_data %>%
        mutate(TEMP_PC = as.integer(PC)) %>%
        left_join(select(conv_matching, c("Postal.code","Refnis.code")), by = c("TEMP_PC" = "Postal.code")) %>%
        left_join(select(refnis, c("NIS_MUN", "MUNICIPALITY", "REGION")), by = c("Refnis.code" = "NIS_MUN")) %>%
        left_join(select(pop, c("NIS.code", "Totaal")), by = c("Refnis.code" = "NIS.code")) %>%
        rename(
            REFNIS = Refnis.code,
            MUNICIPALITY = MUNICIPALITY,
            REGION = REGION,
            POPULATION = Totaal
        ) %>%
        select(-TEMP_PC) %>%
        mutate(
            POPULATION = as.numeric(gsub("\\.", "", POPULATION)),
        ) %>%
        mutate(
            POPULATION = ifelse(is.na(POPULATION), mean(POPULATION, na.rm = TRUE), POPULATION)
        )
    if (any(duplicated(output_data$ID))) {stop("Duplicated IDs found in enriched_data")}
    if (nrow(output_data) != nrow(input_data)) {stop("Row count mismatch between enriched_data and raw_data")}    
    return(output_data)
}

# Preparation recipe

data_preparation_recipe <- function(input_data) {
    if (!exists("original_categorical_features")) {stop("original_categorical_features object is missing")}
    if (!exists("levels_named_list")) {stop("levels_named_list object is missing")}
    if (!exists("result_named_list")) {stop("result_named_list object is missing")}
    if (!exists("n_bins_named_list")) {stop("n_bins_named_list object is missing")}
    if (!exists("binned_continuous_features")) {stop("binned_continuous_features object is missing")}
    if (!exists("binned_enriched_features")) {stop("binned_enriched_features object is missing")}

    # Ensure all required columns are present in the input data
    factor_features <- c(original_categorical_features, binned_continuous_features)
    base_features <- unique(gsub("_binned|_merged", "", binned_continuous_features))
    required_columns <- c(original_categorical_features, base_features)
    missing_columns <- setdiff(required_columns, colnames(input_data))
    if (length(missing_columns) > 0) {
        stop(sprintf("Columns missing from input_data: %s", paste(missing_columns, collapse = ", ")))
    }

    # Set all original categorical features as factors
    rec <- recipe(~ ., data = input_data, strings_as_factors = FALSE) %>%
        step_mutate(
            across(all_of(!!original_categorical_features), as.factor)
        )

    # Bin the continuous features
    for (col in c(base_features, "POPULATION")) {
        n_bins <- n_bins_named_list[[col]]
        if (is.null(result_named_list[[col]]) || is.null(n_bins)) {
            stop(sprintf("Binning configuration is missing for column %s", col))
        }
        bins <- rebuild_bins(result_named_list[[col]], n_bins)
        if (length(bins) != n_bins + 1 || anyNA(bins) || any(diff(bins) <= 0)) {
            stop(sprintf("Invalid bin boundaries for column %s", col))
        }
        rec <- rec %>%
            step_mutate(
                !!paste0(col, "_binned") := cut(
                    !!rlang::sym(col), breaks = !!bins,
                    ordered_result = TRUE, include.lowest = TRUE
                )
            )
    }

    # Merge specific binned categories into broader categories
    rec <- rec %>%
        step_mutate(
            AGEPH_binned_merged = fct_collapse(
                AGEPH_binned, "(66,95]" = c("(66,68]", "(68,71]", "(71,95]")
            ),
            POWER_binned_merged = fct_collapse(
                POWER_binned, "(76,243]" = c("(76,83]", "(83,99]", "(99,243]")
            ),
            REGION_merged = fct_collapse(
                fct_expand(
                    as.factor(REGION), "RÉGION DE BRUXELLES-CAPITALE",
                    "RÉGION WALLONNE", "RÉGION FLAMANDE"
                ),
                "Brussels" = "RÉGION DE BRUXELLES-CAPITALE",
                "Others" = c("RÉGION WALLONNE", "RÉGION FLAMANDE")
            ),
            MUNICIPALITY_binned = factor(ifelse(
                MUNICIPALITY %in% !!levels_named_list[["MUNICIPALITY_binned"]],
                as.character(MUNICIPALITY), "Other"
            ))
        )

    # Set factor levels based on predefined levels_named_list and ensure they are unordered and with the correct reference level
    for (col in c(factor_features, "REGION_merged", "MUNICIPALITY_binned", "POPULATION_binned")) {
        feature_levels <- levels_named_list[[col]]
        if (is.null(feature_levels) || length(feature_levels) == 0) {
            stop(sprintf("Factor levels are missing for column %s", col))
        }
        factor_expression <- rlang::expr(factor(
            !!rlang::sym(col), levels = !!feature_levels, ordered = FALSE
        ))
        rec <- rec %>%
            step_mutate(!!!setNames(list(factor_expression), col)) %>%
            step_relevel(!!rlang::sym(col), ref_level = feature_levels[1])
    }

    # Add the two specific in
    rec <- rec %>%
        step_mutate(
            BM_01_FUEL_gasoline = BM_binned == "[0,1]" & FUEL == "gasoline",
            BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline = BM_binned == "[0,1]" & FUEL != "gasoline"
        ) %>% prep()
    return(rec)
}

data_preparation_workflow <- function(input_data) {
    enriched_data <- data_enrichment(input_data)
    prepared_recipe <- data_preparation_recipe(enriched_data)
    output_data <- bake(prepared_recipe, new_data = enriched_data)
    return(output_data)
}
```
```{r test_data_preparation_enriched}
test_data <- mtpl_be %>%
    filter(ID %in% data$ID) %>%
    data_preparation_workflow()

# Set ordered factors for binned continuous features to unordered
for (col in names(levels_named_list)) {
    data_enriched[[col]] <- factor(data_enriched[[col]], levels = levels_named_list[[col]], ordered = FALSE)
}

prepared_features <- unique(c(
    original_categorical_features, binned_continuous_features,
    enriched_features, binned_enriched_features,
    "BM_01_FUEL_gasoline", "BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline"
))
for (col in prepared_features) {
    if (!col %in% colnames(test_data)) {
        stop(paste("Column", col, "is missing from test_data"))
    }
    if (!identical(test_data[[col]], data_enriched[[col]])) {
        stop(paste("Column", col, "does not match the enriched data"))
    }
}

cat(sprintf("All columns in test_data match the enriched data.\n(%s)", paste(c(original_categorical_features, binned_continuous_features, enriched_features), collapse = ", ")))
```

The preparation workflow works as expected and returns the same dataset as the one obtained throught data preparation. 
As this data transformation is the base for all subsequent modeling steps, we apply it once and we will reuse the prepared data throughout the analysis.

### Performance Evaluation

To robustly evaluate the performance of our models, we will use a 5-fold cross-validation approach. This means that 5 samples will be created from the training data (with the number of claims as evenly distributed as possible across the folds).
Then, for each of the five folds, one fold will be used as the validation set while the remaining four folds will be used as the training set. The performance metrics will then be computed for slight variations in the training and validation sets, providing a more robust estimate of model performance.

More specifically, we will look at two different cross-validation metrics: the log-loss and the (decomposed) prediction error.

1. Cross-Validated `Log-loss`

The log-loss is a measure based on the likelihood of the observed data given the predicted probabilities. 
The negative mean log-likelihood is used as the loss function. Note that the likelihood function depends on the assumed distribution poisson(log) or gamma(log)).
For our frequency model, which assumes a Poisson distribution with a log link, the log-loss will then be:

$$
\text{Log-loss} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \log \left( P(Y_i \mid \hat{\lambda}_i) \right)
$$
where \(Y_i\) is the observed number of claims for the \(i\)-th observation, and \(\hat{\lambda}_i\) is the predicted mean from the Poisson model.

The function `dpois` in R will be used with `NCLAIMS` as the observed values and the predicted mean from the Poisson model as the lambda parameter. We'll use log=TRUE to get the log-probabilities and be able to average them and then take the negative to compute the log-loss.

2. Cross-Validated `Prediction error`

The prediction error is a measure of the difference between the observed and predicted values for new data points that can be split between the training error and the optimism (difference between training and prediction error which can be seen as a complexity penalty):

$$
\mathbb{E}[(Y_i^{\text{new}} - \hat{Y}_i)^2] = \mathbb{E}[(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2] + 2 Cov(Y_i, \hat{Y}_i)
$$

The training error can be replaced by the deviance \(D\), which measures the goodness of fit of the model to the training data. The optimism term \(2 Cov(Y_i, \hat{Y}_i)\) can be approximated by the penalty term \(\frac{2(p+1)}{n}\), where \(p\) is the number of parameters and \(n\) is the sample size.

$$
\text{Prediction error} = D + \frac{2(p+1)}{n} 
$$

Therefore, the sum of prediction errors across all observations can be expressed as:

$$
\text{Total Prediction Error} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( D_i + \frac{2(p+1)}{n} \right) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} D_i + 2(p+1)
$$

We will also log the deviance and complexity penalty separately to interpret the contribution of each to the overall prediction error.

The log loss should simply indicate how close we are getting to the true distribution whereas the prediction error focuses on the accuracy of the predicted values for new observations with a complexity penalty to avoid overfitting.
Comparing both should help us picking the most balanced model. 

3. `Information Criteria`

To confirm the prediction error, we will also look at the AIC and BIC on the full training data model. 
These information criteria are also built on the likelihood of the model and a penalty for model complexity (AIC uses `2 * k` and BIC uses `log(n) * k`, where `k` is the number of parameters and `n` is the sample size).
They should thus provide similar ranking as the cross-validated prediction error with possible divergence due to the different ways complexity is penalized.

4. `Nested Model Comparison`

At the end of each complexity layer (set of covariates added), we will compare the current model with the previous best model with an anova test to evaluate whether the addition of new covariates significantly improves the model fit.
The anova test is based on the comparison of the deviance of nested models, which follows a chi-squared distribution under the null hypothesis that the simpler model is sufficient.

- Null Deviance: $D_0 = 2 \times \left( logLik(SaturatedModel) - logLik(NullModel) \right)$
- Residual Deviance: $D_m = 2 \times \left( logLik(SaturatedModel) - logLik(FittedModel) \right)$

Let's visualize the link between deviance and log-likelihood for the nested models: null and model with BM_binned covariate. Calculated deviance should match the residual deviance for each model and is defined as $D_m = 2 \times \left( logLik(SaturatedModel) - logLik(FittedModel) \right)$.

```{r full_model_deviance}
train_data <- mtpl_be %>%
    filter(ID %in% data$ID) %>%
    data_preparation_workflow()
m_null <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)), family = poisson, data = train_data)
m_ex <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)) + BM_binned, family = poisson, data = train_data)

ll_null <- logLik(m_null)
ll_ex <- logLik(m_ex)
d_null <- deviance(m_null)
d_ex <- deviance(m_ex)
ll_sat <- d_null/2 + ll_null
d_sat <- 0
calc_d_null <- 2 * (ll_sat - ll_null)
calc_d_ex <- 2 * (ll_sat - ll_ex)

data.frame(
    Model = c("Null", "Saturated", "BM_binned"),
    LogLik = c(as.numeric(ll_null), as.numeric(ll_sat), as.numeric(ll_ex)),
    Deviance = c(d_null, d_sat, d_ex),
    Calculated_Deviance = c(calc_d_null, d_sat, calc_d_ex)
) %>% kable(
    caption = "Example Deviance and Log-Likelihood for Nested Models",
    booktabs = TRUE
)
rm(ll_null, ll_ex, d_null, d_ex, ll_sat, d_sat, calc_d_null, calc_d_ex)
```

The Chi-squared anova test will be comparing the difference of the deviance of the nested models to evaluate whether the addition of new covariates significantly improves the model fit:

The test statistic is calculated as $\chi^2 = D_0 - D_m$

where $D_0$ is the deviance of the null model and $D_m$ is the deviance of the model with additional covariates. Under the null hypothesis, this statistic follows a chi-squared distribution with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in the number of parameters between the models.
The null hypothesis states that the simpler model is sufficient, meaning that the additional covariates do not significantly improve the model fit. Concretely, if the p-value from the chi-squared test is lower than our chosen significance level of 5%, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the additional covariates significantly improve the model fit.
The more complex model becomes our new best model benchmark and we move on to the next complexity layer.

```{r anova_test}
anova(m_null, m_ex, test = "Chisq")
rm(m_null, m_ex)
```

Note how the residual deviances are aligned with the one we calculated. The `BM_binned` adds two additional dummy variables (as it has three levels with one as the reference category).
The test statistic is then $D_0 - D_m$ with 2 degrees of freedom. The probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one calculated under the null hypothesis is given by the p-value from the chi-squared test.

## Frequency GLM Workflow

We have already covered the data preparation and performance metrics choice for our workflow. The final decision is the specification of the model formula we will choose.
We will use the poisson family with a log link function for modeling the frequency of claims because:

- The `NCLAIMS` variable represents count data, which is naturally modeled using a Poisson distribution.
- The log link function has multiple advantages:
    - It is the canonical link for the Poisson distribution, ensuring the property of the method of marginal totals (the sum of the fitted values equals the sum of the observed values).
    - It guarantees that the predicted values are always positive, which is appropriate for count data.
    - It allows for a multiplicative interpretation of the effects of covariates on the expected count which is easier to understand and communicate to the business.

```{r glm_workflow}

create_wflow_freq_glm <- function(data, formula, v = 5, rec=recipe(NCLAIMS ~ ., data = data), seed = 123) {

    set.seed(seed)
    folds <- vfold_cv(
        data, 
        v = v, 
        strata = NCLAIMS
    )

    mod <- poisson_reg() %>%
        set_engine("glm")

    wflow <- workflow() %>%
        add_recipe(rec) %>%
        add_model(mod, formula = as.formula(formula))

    cv_results <- fit_resamples(
        wflow,
        resamples = folds,
        control = control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE)
    )

    # Fit the final model on the training data
    final_fit <- fit(wflow, data = data)
    glm_fit <- extract_fit_engine(final_fit)

    # Compute the cross-validated metrics
    cv_pred <- collect_predictions(cv_results)

    cv_metrics <- cv_pred %>%
        mutate(
            deviance_i = poisson()$dev.resids(
                y = NCLAIMS, mu = .pred, wt = 1
            ),
            log_loss_i = -dpois(
                NCLAIMS, lambda = .pred, log = TRUE
            )
        ) %>%
        summarise(
            CV_Deviance = sum(deviance_i),
            CV_LogLoss = mean(log_loss_i)
        )

    n <- nrow(data)
    k <- glm_fit$rank  # fitted parameters, including the intercept
    training_deviance <- cv_metrics$CV_Deviance
    complexity_penalty <- 2 * k
    estimated_prediction_error <- training_deviance + complexity_penalty

    list(
        workflow = wflow,
        fit = glm_fit,
        performance_metrics = list(
            AIC = AIC(glm_fit),
            BIC = BIC(glm_fit),
            Deviance = deviance(glm_fit),
            CV_Deviance = cv_metrics$CV_Deviance,
            CV_Complexity = complexity_penalty,
            CV_Prediction_Error = estimated_prediction_error,
            CV_LogLoss = cv_metrics$CV_LogLoss
        )
    )
}
```

The workflow that we will use for the frequency modelling using GLM(poisson) includes the following steps:

1. Specify the 5-fold cross-validation
2. Specify the Poisson regression model with a log link
3. Fit the model on the entire training dataset
4. Perform cross-validation to evaluate cv performance metrics
5. Return the workflow, fitted model, and performance metrics

This workflow will be used for all models in the frequency analysis, ensuring consistency in model fitting, cross-validation, and performance evaluation.

### Categorical Variables Only

Let us start with adding the categorical variables only to our frequency model:

- `COVERAGE`
- `FLEET`
- `SEX`
- `FUEL`

Note that `USE` was not significant in the preliminary analysis and thus is not included in the categorical variables for the frequency model.

```{r categorical_variables}
perf_metrics_df <- data.frame(
    Model = character(),
    AIC = numeric(),
    BIC = numeric(),
    Deviance = numeric(),
    CV_Deviance = numeric(),
    CV_Complexity = numeric(),
    CV_Prediction_Error = numeric(),
    CV_LogLoss = numeric(),
    Formula = character()
)

append_performance_metrics <- function(name, formula,result, perf_df = perf_metrics_df) {
    perf <- result$performance_metrics
    new_row <- data.frame(
        Model = name,
        AIC = perf$AIC,
        BIC = perf$BIC,
        Deviance = perf$Deviance,
        CV_Deviance = perf$CV_Deviance,
        CV_Complexity = perf$CV_Complexity,
        CV_Prediction_Error = perf$CV_Prediction_Error,
        CV_LogLoss = perf$CV_LogLoss,
        Formula = formula
    )
    rbind(perf_df, new_row)
}

f0 <- "NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP))"
fcat <- paste0(f0, " + ", paste(original_categorical_features, collapse = " + "))
cat(sprintf("> Categorical formula: %s", fcat))

r0 <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, f0)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "Intercept Only", formula = f0, result = r0)
rcat <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, fcat)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "Categorical Only", formula = fcat, result = rcat)

perf_metrics_df %>% arrange(CV_Prediction_Error) %>% select(-Formula) %>% knitr::kable(
    booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Performance Metrics for Frequency Models After Adding Categorical Variables"
)
```

```{r summary_rcat_fit}
test <- anova(r0$fit, rcat$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Is the categorical model a significant improvement over the intercept-only model? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))

delta_deviance <- r0$performance_metrics$CV_Deviance - rcat$performance_metrics$CV_Deviance
diff_degree_of_freedom <- r0$fit$df.residual - rcat$fit$df.residual
pvalue <- pchisq(delta_deviance, diff_degree_of_freedom, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat(sprintf("Anova test based on CV Deviance: delta_deviance = %.4f, diff_degree_of_freedom = %d, p-value = %.4f\n", delta_deviance, diff_degree_of_freedom, pvalue))

check_summary <- function(result) {
    sum_mod <- summary(result$fit)
    coefficients <- sum_mod$coefficients %>% as.data.frame()
    coefficients$p.value <- coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
    coefficients <- coefficients %>% select(Estimate, `Std. Error`, p.value)
    coefficients$significant <- ifelse(coefficients$p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No")
    coefficients$multiplier <- exp(coefficients[, "Estimate"])
    coefficients$multiplier_lb <- exp(coefficients[, "Estimate"] - 1.96 * coefficients[, "Std. Error"])
    coefficients$multiplier_ub <- exp(coefficients[, "Estimate"] + 1.96 * coefficients[, "Std. Error"])
    return(coefficients)
}

plot_summary <- function(result, add_text=FALSE) {
    coefficients <- check_summary(result) 
    mult_df <- coefficients %>% filter(rownames(coefficients) != "(Intercept)")
    ggplot(mult_df, aes(x = rownames(mult_df), y = multiplier, ymin = multiplier_lb, ymax = multiplier_ub)) +
        geom_pointrange(
            color = ifelse(mult_df$significant == "Yes", "black", "firebrick")
        ) +
        geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
        {if(add_text) geom_text(
            aes(label = round(multiplier, 2)), vjust = 2, 
            color = ifelse(mult_df$multiplier > 1, "firebrick", "darkgreen")
        ) else NULL} +
        coord_flip() +
        labs(x = "Coefficient", y = "Multiplier", title = sprintf("Coefficient Multipliers and 95%% CI\nClaim frequency of the reference category: %.2f", exp(result$fit$coefficients[1]))) +
        theme_minimal()
}
coefs <- check_summary(rcat)
plot_summary(rcat, add_text=TRUE)
```

We see that the anova test indicates that the more complex model with categorical variables is a significant improvement over the intercept-only model.
We also observe that all the levels we kept are significant. The multipliers are in line with our expectations based on the data exploration:

- Female drivers have a higher risk compared to male drivers: the multiplier for the female category is of `r coefs["SEXfemale", "multiplier"]` (95% CI: `r coefs["SEXfemale", "multiplier_lb"]` - `r coefs["SEXfemale", "multiplier_ub"]`)
- Diesel cars are significantly more risky compared to gasoline cars: the multiplier for the diesel category is of `r coefs["FUELdiesel", "multiplier"]` (95% CI: `r coefs["FUELdiesel", "multiplier_lb"]` - `r coefs["FUELdiesel", "multiplier_ub"]`)
- Cars that are part of a fleet have a lower risk compared to non-fleet cars: the multiplier for the fleet category is of `r coefs["FLEETY", "multiplier"]` (95% CI: `r coefs["FLEETY", "multiplier_lb"]` - `r coefs["FLEETY", "multiplier_ub"]`)
- Drivers with an omnium coverage are at a lower risk compared to those with TPL only: the multiplier for the omnium category is of `r coefs["COVERAGE_BINOMN", "multiplier"]` (95% CI: `r coefs["COVERAGE_BINOMN", "multiplier_lb"]` - `r coefs["COVERAGE_BINOMN", "multiplier_ub"]`)

We can conclude that the categorical variables were well-chosen in the EDA and have a significant impact in our model.
The new model is better than the null model and needs no adaptation, so we can continue with the `rcat` model as our new baseline for further model development.

```{r reassign_rcat}
base_mod <- rcat
base_f <- fcat
```

### Adding Binned Continuous Variables

Next, we will add the binned continuous variables to our model to capture the potential non-linear effects of continuous predictors on the frequency of claims:

- BM_binned
- AGEPH_binned_merged
- AGEC_binned
- POWER_binned_merged

```{r binned_continuous_variables}
fcontb <- paste0(base_f, " + ", paste(binned_continuous_features, collapse = " + "))
cat(sprintf("> Full formula with binned continuous variables: %s", fcontb))

rcontb <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, fcontb)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "All Continuous Binned", formula = fcontb, result = rcontb)

test <- anova(base_mod$fit, rcontb$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Is the full model with binned continuous variables a significant improvement over the categorical model? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))

coefs_contb <- check_summary(rcontb)
plot_summary(rcontb)
```

There are three main takeaways from the analysis of this more complex model:

1. With the addition of binned continuous variables, the `SEXfemale` variable is just barely significant, we can test whether the nested anova test supports its removal from the model.
2. The binned continuous variables themselves are all significant at the 95% confidence level. The WoE-based binning and merging strategy we applied is therefore effective in capturing significant non-linear effects of continuous predictors on the frequency of claims.
3. Some coefficients of the binned variables are very similar, we'll consider merging them later for the final model.

Let's proceed to remove the `SEX` variable from the model and evaluate the impact on model performance.

```{r prune_cont_mod}
large_mod <- rcontb$fit
fcontb_rsex <- gsub(" \\+ SEX", "", fcontb)
cat(sprintf("> Formula after removing SEX: %s", fcontb_rsex))

rcontb_rsex <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, fcontb_rsex)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "Continuous Binned without SEX", formula = fcontb_rsex, result = rcontb_rsex)
test_p2 <- anova(large_mod, rcontb_rsex$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Are we loosing significant explanatory power by removing SEX? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_p2$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_p2$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
coefs_contb_p2 <- check_summary(rcontb_rsex)
perf_metrics_df %>% arrange(CV_Prediction_Error) %>% select(-Formula) %>% kable(
    booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Performance Metrics for Frequency Models After Removing SEX"
)
base_f <- fcontb
base_mod <- rcontb
```

We see with that based on the prediction error, our best model includes the SEX. The complexity cost of 2 is justified by the reduction in deviance (confirmed by AIC). 
The anova test also confirms that removing the SEX variable results in a significant loss of explanatory power. Only the BIC criteria favors the simpler model as complexity is penalized more heavily.
We will keep the SEX variable in our best model benchmark and continue with the next layer of covariates.

### Enriched Features

After including our continuous binned variables, we will now add the new geospatial and enriched features:

- `REGION_merged`
- `MUNICIPALITY_binned`
- `POPULATION_binned`

Because the bins in `MUNICIPALITY_binned` are very small, they will not do well with cross-validation, so we will focus on the other two enriched features and then test the impact of including `MUNICIPALITY_binned` without cross-validation.

```{r enriched_features}
f_enr2 <- paste0(base_f, " + REGION_merged + POPULATION_binned")
cat(sprintf("> Formula after adding two enriched features: %s", f_enr2))
r_enr2 <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, f_enr2)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "Enriched Features", formula = f_enr2, result = r_enr2)
test_enr2 <- anova(base_mod$fit, r_enr2$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Are we gaining significant explanatory power by adding enriched features? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_enr2$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_enr2$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
coefs_enr2 <- check_summary(r_enr2)
plot_summary(r_enr2)
```

We notice that the `REGION_merged` and `POPULATION_binned` variables contribute significantly to the model, it was therefore worth including them as enriched features in our final model.

- `REGION_mergedBrussels` is actually the second highest multiplier of claim frequency in the model: `r coefs_enr2["REGION_mergedBrussels", "multiplier"]` (95% CI: `r coefs_enr2["REGION_mergedBrussels", "multiplier_lb"]` - `r coefs_enr2["REGION_mergedBrussels", "multiplier_ub"]`)
- The two largest bins in `POPULATION_binned` have significant but similar coefficients, we will also consider merging them in the final model section.

Finally, let's have a quick look at the `MUNICIPALITY_binned` variable to see if it can add anything to the urban and population density we already considered.
Note that we won't use our workflow because the bins are too small and we will run into issues with non-observed levels in the cross-validation folds.
We'll make a single GLM fit to test our hypothesis.

```{r municipality_binned}
f_enr3 <- paste0(f_enr2, " + MUNICIPALITY_binned")
cat(sprintf("> Formula after adding MUNICIPALITY_binned: %s", f_enr3))
r_enr3 <- list()
r_enr3$fit <- glm(as.formula(f_enr3), data = train_data, family = poisson())
test_enr3 <- anova(r_enr2$fit, r_enr3$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Does MUNICIPALITY_binned add significant explanatory power? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_enr3$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_enr3$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
coefs_enr3 <- check_summary(r_enr3)
plot_summary(r_enr3)
# base_mod <- r_enr2$fit
```

The interpretation of the `MUNICIPALITY_binned` effect on the model is difficult. We first see that the effet of La Louvière, Charleroi, and Anvers are not significant. Only Mons is significant but barely.
What is more interesting to notice is that we only have four out of the six original municipalities. This is because of `collinearity`. As we explained in the feature engineering section, adding similar views of the geographical location yields redundant information and the model automatically drops some levels to avoid perfect multicollinearity.
We can dive deeper in this issue with the `alias` function in R, which shows which coefficients are linearly dependent and therefore dropped from the model.

```{r alias_municipality}
alias_mat <- alias(r_enr3$fit)$Complete
alias_mat[, colSums(abs(alias_mat)) > 0] %>% kable(
    caption = "Alias matrix for MUNICIPALITY_binned"
)
```

Taking the example of Gand, this means that we know the policyholder lived in Gand in 1997 because he live in a municipality with a population between 20500 and 45300 people that is not Anvers.
We can prove that by filtering our training data based on these criteria:

```{r filter_gand}
train_data %>%
  filter(POPULATION_binned == "(2.05e+05,4.53e+05]", MUNICIPALITY_binned != "Anvers") %>%
  select(MUNICIPALITY_binned) %>%
  unique() %>%
  kable(
    caption = "MUNICIPALITY_binned values for the filtered criteria"
  )
```

Even if adding the `MUNICIPALITY_binned` variable to the model adds some explanatory power, it creates multicollinearity issues and provides a single, barely interpretable coefficient for Mons.
We will therefore not include the `MUNICIPALITY_binned` variable in our best model and continue with only the two other features.

```{r base_model_after_enriched}
base_f <- f_enr2
base_mod <- r_enr2
```

### Interaction Effects

The final complexity layer for this GLM estimation chapter for the claim frequency model is to include the interaction effects we identified with the decision tree analysis.

- `BM_binned` x `AGEPH_binned_merged`
- `REGION_merged` x `POWER_binned_merged`
- `BM_binned` x `REGION_merged`
- `BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline`
- `BM_01_FUEL_gasoline`

The interaction based on expert knowledge will also be considered:

- `AGEPH_binned_merged` x `POWER_binned_merged`

Because interactions will create very small cross sections, we'll skip cross validation and use a single GLM estimation.

```{r interactions}
f_int <- paste0(base_f, " + ", paste(interaction_features, collapse = " + "))
cat(sprintf("> Formula after adding specific interaction: %s", f_int))
r_int <- list()
r_int$fit <- glm(as.formula(f_int), data = train_data, family = poisson())
test_int <- anova(base_mod$fit, r_int$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Are we gaining significant explanatory power by adding interactions? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_int$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_int$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
coefs_int <- check_summary(r_int)
plot_summary(r_int)
```

Note that even if the interactions add some explanatory power, they make the model more complex, less stable, and harder to interpret.
The region Brussels for example does not have a significant effect anymore as it is included in the interaction terms and confounded with other variables.
Besides, only the specific BM between 1 and 11 x Brussels Region has a significant effect on claim frequency.
We can focus on the two specific interactions only to see if we can have a more interpretable and stable model.

```{r interactions_specific}
f_sp_int <- paste0(base_f, " + BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline + BM_01_FUEL_gasoline")
cat(sprintf("> Formula after adding specific interaction: %s", f_sp_int))
r_sp_int <- list()
r_sp_int$fit <- glm(as.formula(f_sp_int), data = train_data, family = poisson())
test_sp_int <- anova(base_mod$fit, r_sp_int$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Are we gaining significant explanatory power by adding interactions? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_sp_int$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_sp_int$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
coefs_sp_int <- check_summary(r_sp_int)
plot_summary(r_sp_int)
```

The `BM_01_FUEL_gasoline` = True is a linear combination of other covariates that are present in the model and is excluded due to perfect multicollinearity.
The other specific interaction `BM_01_FUEL_not_gasoline` = True is not significant. We will therefore not include these specific interactions either.
Based on this complexity layer approach, we can select the enriched model as our best model as far. In the last part of this GLM modeling, we will summarize the performance metrics and prune the best model for similar coefficients.

### Selection of the Best Model

We can close the GLM frequency model estimation here by looking at the evolution of our performance metrics across the different modeling stages:

```{r performance_metrics}

perf_metrics_df %>% arrange(CV_Prediction_Error) %>% select(-Formula) %>% kable(
    booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Final Leaderboard ordered by CV Prediction Error"
)
plot_leaderboard <- function(data, metric, title, digits = 2) {

    plot_data <- data %>%
        transmute(
            Model = as.character(Model),
            value = .data[[metric]]
        ) %>%
        arrange(desc(value)) %>%
        mutate(
            Model = factor(Model, levels = Model),
            best = value == min(value, na.rm = TRUE)
        )

    ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = value, y = Model)) +
        geom_segment(
            aes(x = min(value), xend = value, yend = Model),
            colour = "grey75"
        ) +
        geom_point(aes(colour = best), size = 3) +
        geom_text(
            aes(label = formatC(value, format = "f", digits = digits)),
            hjust = -0.15,
            size = 3.3
        ) +
        scale_colour_manual(
            values = c("FALSE" = "grey", "TRUE" = "darkgreen"),
            guide = "none"
        ) +
        scale_x_continuous(
            expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.35))
        ) +
        labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = NULL) +
        # remove x-axis labels
        theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
        theme(
            panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
            panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
            plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
            axis.text.x = element_blank()
        )
}

p1 <- plot_leaderboard(perf_metrics_df, "AIC", "AIC")
p2 <- plot_leaderboard(perf_metrics_df, "BIC", "BIC")
p3 <- plot_leaderboard(perf_metrics_df, "CV_Prediction_Error", "CV Prediction Error")
p4 <- plot_leaderboard(
    perf_metrics_df, "CV_LogLoss", "CV Log Loss", digits = 4
)

(p1 | p2) / (p3 | p4) +
    plot_annotation(
        title = "Model performance leaderboard",
        subtitle = "Best model highlighted in green"
)
```

Based on this leaderboard, we can confirm that our final model with categorical, significant binned continuous features and significant enriched features performs the best across all evaluated metrics.
The other models have the same ranking across AIC, cross-validated prediction error, and cross-validated Poisson log loss. The only difference we noticed is in the BIC metric that penalizes more model complexity.
The penalisation coefficient is sufficiently large to prefer the model with continuous bins without sex to the one with sex included.

Now that we have identified the best-performing model, can we proceed to merge levels with similar effects without losing predictive power?

```{r merge_levels}
plot_summary(base_mod)
```

Visual inspection points towards the following potential merges:

1. `POPULATION_binned`: (1.34e+05,2.05e+05] and (2.05e+05,4.53e+05]
2. `COVERAGE`: PO and FO under OM for omnium
3. `POWER_binned`: (47-51] and (51-76]

We will adapt the recipe in our workflow to implement these potential merges and evaluate their impact on model performance one by one.

```{r potential_merges_population}
rec_pop <- recipe(NCLAIMS ~ ., data = train_data) %>%
    step_mutate(
        POPULATION_binned = fct_collapse(POPULATION_binned,
            "(1.34e+05,4.53e+05]" = c("(1.34e+05,2.05e+05]", "(2.05e+05,4.53e+05]")
        )
    )
r_mpop <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, base_f, rec = rec_pop)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "Merged POPULATION_binned", formula = base_f, result = r_mpop)
test_mpop <- anova(base_mod$fit, r_mpop$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Are we gaining significant explanatory power by keeping the levels separate? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_mpop$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_mpop$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
```

Merging the `POPULATION_binned` levels (1.34e+05,2.05e+05] and (2.05e+05,4.53e+05] into a single level (1.34e+05,4.53e+05] allows us to simplify the model without losing significant explanatory power, as indicated by the p-value from the likelihood ratio test.
Let's proceed with the coverage variable. We already identified in the data exploration that the `PO` and `FO` could potentially be merged under the `OM` level for omnium coverage.

```{r potential_merges_coverage}
base_mod <- r_mpop
rec_cov <- rec_pop %>%
    step_mutate(
        COVERAGE = fct_collapse(COVERAGE,
            "OM" = c("PO", "FO")
        )
    )
r_mcov <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, base_f, rec = rec_cov)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "Merged COVERAGE", formula = base_f, result = r_mcov)
test_mcov <- anova(base_mod$fit, r_mcov$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Are we gaining significant explanatory power by keeping the COVERAGE levels separate? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_mcov$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_mcov$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
```

Again, merging the `COVERAGE` levels `PO` and `FO` into a single `OM` level simplifies the model without a significant loss of explanatory power, as indicated by the p-value from the likelihood ratio test.
Let's continue with our third and last potential merge for the `POWER_binned` variable.

```{r potential_merges_power}
base_mod <- r_mcov
rec_pow <- rec_cov %>%
    step_mutate(
        POWER_binned_merged = fct_collapse(POWER_binned_merged,
            "(47,76]" = c("(47,51]","(51,76]")
        )
    )
r_mpow <- create_wflow_freq_glm(train_data, base_f, rec = rec_pow)
perf_metrics_df <- append_performance_metrics(name = "Merged POWER_binned", formula = base_f, result = r_mpow)
test_mpow <- anova(base_mod$fit, r_mpow$fit, test = "Chisq")
cat(sprintf("Are we gaining significant explanatory power by keeping the POWER_binned levels separate? %s (p-value = %.4f)\n", ifelse(test_mpow$`Pr(>Chi)`[2] < 0.05, "Yes", "No"), test_mpow$`Pr(>Chi)`[2]))
```

It seems that all merges make sense. Let's visualize the performance and coefficients of our final best GLM model.

```{r final_glm_visualization}
base_mod <- r_mpow
base_rec <- rec_pow

plot_summary(base_mod)
perf_metrics_df %>% arrange(CV_Prediction_Error) %>% select(-Formula) %>% kable(
    booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Final Leaderboard after levels merging ordered by CV Prediction Error"
)
```

Our final best GLM model is the simplified one with merged `COVERAGE`, `POWER_binned` and `POPULATION_levels`.
The CV Complexity obviously favors this simplified model, but even the cross-validated deviance and log loss are slightly better which indicates that the model generalizes better.
We will take this model as the base for our subsequent GAM exploration.


<br>

## Frequency GAM Workflow

With our best GLM model as basis, we will explore whether incorporating smoothed terms for continuous variables instead of using bins can improve model performance.

### Smoothing Example for Spatial Effect

To illustrate the power of smoothing, we will compare the coefficients and significance of `LONG` in `LAT` when used in a GLM versus a GAM.
Note that in the GAM[^bam], we will use the bivariate smooth term `s(LONG, LAT)` to capture the spatial effect and not the tensor product smooth `te(LONG, LAT)` becayse the two variables have the same units (isotropic).

[^bam]: The `bam` function from the `mgcv` package is used to fit generalized additive models with potentially large datasets efficiently, utilizing parallel computation when specified.

```{r smoothing_example}
glm_long_lat <- glm(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)) + LONG + LAT, data = train_data, family = poisson())
summary(glm_long_lat)$coefficients %>% kable(
    booktabs = TRUE, caption = "GLM Coefficients for LONG and LAT"
)

cl <- makeCluster(detectCores() - 1)
bam_freq_long_lat <- bam(NCLAIMS ~ offset(log(EXP)) + s(LONG, LAT), data = train_data, family = poisson(), cluster = cl)
stopCluster(cl)
summary(bam_freq_long_lat)$s.table %>%
    kable(
        booktabs = TRUE,
        caption = "Approximate significance of spatial smooth"
    )

vis.gam(
    bam_freq_long_lat, view = c("LONG", "LAT"), plot.type = "contour", type="response",
    main = "Predicted Frequency in Belgium", cond = list(EXP = 1)
)
maps::map("world", regions = "Belgium", add = TRUE, col = "white", lwd = 2)
points(
    x = c(4.3517, 5.5797),
    y = c(50.8503, 50.6326),
    col = "red", pch = 19, cex = 1.2
)
text(
    x = c(4.3517, 5.5797),
    y = c(50.8503, 50.6326),
    labels = c("Brussels", "Liège"),
    pos = 3, col = "red", cex = 0.9
)
```

From a statistical perspective, the GAM yields a far more significant predictor with the spatial smooth term `s(LONG, LAT)` compared to the individual coefficients for `LONG` (not even significant) and `LAT` in the GLM.
But more importantly, the non-linear spatial effect can be visualized and interpreted, showing for example that frequency is a lot higher around Brussels (as we see with the `REGION` variable in the GLM) and close to Liège.
When adding this smooth term to the model, we can guess that the predictive power of the variable `REGION_merged` will decrease, as the sur-frequency around the capital is already captured by the spatial smooth term.
It is also lower in rural parts of the country namely in the Ardennes and other sparsely populated areas.

# Severity Modeling

We went through a lot of details in the data preparation and model selection process for the frequency component of our analysis.
For the severity component, we will go through a similar process in much lesser depth to keep this report concise.
We will nevertheless go through the following steps:

- Filter out non-relevant observations for the severity analysis
- Look at the distribution of the severity across individual features
- Adapt the validation metrics to the Gamma family with a log link
- Compare claim-count weighting of average costs with a claim-count offset for total costs
- Fit, prune, and compare successive GLM layers using cross-validation
- Evaluate the shortlisted models on the holdout set, then simplify and interpret the final model

Watch out that we are not using the canonical link function for the Gamma distribution, which is the inverse link.
This means that the sum of predicted values might not equal the total observed cost. In a real-world setting, we would need to account for this discrepancy when setting premiums.
The reason why we will use the log link instead of the canonical inverse link is to ensure that our predicted values are always positive and to simplify the interpretation of the model coefficients (as multiplicative effects on the expected value of the response variable).

## Validation Framework

### Data Preparation for Severity Analysis

```{r data-prep-severity}
train_severity <- train_data[train_data$NCLAIMS > 0, ]
avg_cost_int <- glm(AVG ~ 1, data = train_severity, family = Gamma(link = "log"))
avg_cost_int_sum <- summary(avg_cost_int)
beta <- avg_cost_int_sum$coefficients[1, 1]
beta_sd <- avg_cost_int_sum$coefficients[1, 2]
cat(sprintf("Estimated mean of average cost: %.2f (95%% CI: %.2f to %.2f)", exp(beta), exp(beta - 1.96 * beta_sd), exp(beta + 1.96 * beta_sd)))
mean_avg <- mean(train_severity$AVG)
sd_avg <- sd(train_severity$AVG)
cat(sprintf("Observed mean of average cost: %.2f (sd-based 95%% CI: %.2f to %.2f)", mean_avg, mean_avg - 1.96 * sd_avg, mean_avg + 1.96 * sd_avg))
```
